questions.stem: In Coleman v Power (2004), a man in Townsville was convicted under a Queensland law of using insulting words when he publicly accused a police officer of corruption. The High Court set aside that conviction. What is the case's significance?
options: It established an express constitutional right for all people to insult public officials
It held that Queensland police officers cannot arrest people for offences involving words
It showed that the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld) overrides any older Queensland law
It confirmed that the implied freedom of political communication also limits state laws
questions.explanation: The Court read the offence narrowly so that it did not catch Coleman's words, with the implied freedom supporting that reading, and the case confirmed the freedom applies to state as well as Commonwealth laws. There is no express right to insult anyone, and the Human Rights Act did not exist in 2004.

questions.stem: In Brown v Tasmania (2017), the High Court held parts of a Tasmanian law invalid. The law let police direct protesters to leave forestry sites and arrest them if they did not. Why was it invalid?
options: It was inconsistent with the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld), which applies in every state
It was made under a power that the Constitution gives exclusively to the Commonwealth
It burdened political communication more than was reasonably necessary to protect businesses
It breached the protesters' express constitutional right to peaceful assembly in section 116
questions.explanation: The Court held that the law's broad and uncertain reach deterred protest well beyond what was needed to stop damage or disruption, so it impermissibly burdened the implied freedom of political communication. The Constitution has no express right of assembly, and section 116 concerns religion.

questions.stem: Under section 5 of the Peaceful Assembly Act 1992 (Qld), a person's right to assemble peacefully with others in a public place is:
options: absolute, so police can never restrict or move on a peaceful assembly in a public place
available only to groups that have obtained a permit from the Supreme Court of Queensland
an express right in the Australian Constitution that the Queensland Parliament cannot change
subject only to restrictions needed for public safety, order or others' rights
questions.explanation: The Act recognises a right of peaceful assembly but allows restrictions that are necessary and reasonable in a democratic society for public safety, public order or the protection of others' rights and freedoms. Because it is an ordinary Act, parliament can amend it.

questions.stem: Organisers give the police and the local council an assembly notice under the Peaceful Assembly Act 1992 (Qld), and the march is authorised. What is the main legal benefit for marchers who follow the notified route and conditions?
options: They cannot be charged with any offence committed during the march
They are entitled to compensation if the march is cancelled by police
They may enter private property along the route without the owner's consent
They are not liable merely for obstructing a public place by taking part
questions.explanation: Section 6 gives participants in an authorised, peaceful assembly held substantially in line with its notified particulars immunity from civil or criminal liability for obstructing a public place. It does not protect people who commit other offences, such as assault or damage.

questions.stem: The Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld) protects freedom of expression (section 21) and peaceful assembly and freedom of association (section 22). Which statement about these protections is correct?
options: They allow courts to declare invalid any Queensland law that limits protest
They apply only to Commonwealth laws and Commonwealth officials in Queensland
They are statutory rights that can be reasonably limited and can be changed by parliament
They are entrenched rights that can be changed only by a referendum of Queensland voters
questions.explanation: The Act is an ordinary statute: section 13 allows rights to be subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified, and parliament can amend or override it. Courts cannot strike down laws for incompatibility; they can only interpret laws compatibly or declare incompatibility.

questions.stem: A Queensland employer refuses to hire an applicant because of his membership of a political party. Which law most clearly makes this unlawful?
options: Section 116 of the Australian Constitution, which protects all beliefs
The Age Discrimination Act 2004 (Cth), which covers all personal attributes
The Anti-Discrimination Act 1991 (Qld), which lists political belief or activity
The Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth), which covers political beliefs
questions.explanation: The Anti-Discrimination Act 1991 (Qld) prohibits discrimination on attributes including political belief or activity, religious belief, trade union activity and family responsibilities. The Commonwealth discrimination Acts each cover particular attributes such as race, sex, disability and age.

questions.stem: A Queensland law requires every public servant to declare their religion. A student says section 116 of the Constitution makes the law invalid. Which response is most accurate?
options: The law is valid, because no Queensland law protects freedom of religion
The law is invalid, because the Anti-Discrimination Act overrides other Queensland Acts
Section 116 binds only the Commonwealth, but the Human Rights Act is relevant
Section 116 makes the law invalid, because it applies to all Australian parliaments
questions.explanation: Section 116 limits only the Commonwealth Parliament. In Queensland, freedom of thought, conscience, religion and belief is protected by section 20 of the Human Rights Act 2019, which affects how laws are interpreted and how public entities act, although it cannot invalidate an Act.

questions.stem: Section 15 of the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld) says that measures taken to assist or advance groups disadvantaged by discrimination do not constitute discrimination. This reflects the idea that:
options: equality means treating every person in exactly the same way
governments may favour any group that they consider deserving
discrimination is lawful whenever a majority of voters supports it
equity may require different treatment to achieve real equality
questions.explanation: Special measures recognise that identical treatment can entrench disadvantage, so targeted support can promote substantive equality. This is the difference between formal equality and equity.

questions.stem: In Rowe v Electoral Commissioner (2010), the High Court held invalid a Commonwealth law that closed the electoral roll on the day an election was called. On what basis?
options: It was inconsistent with the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld), which protects voting rights
It breached section 80, which guarantees trial by jury for electoral offences
It disenfranchised people without a substantial reason, contrary to sections 7 and 24
It breached section 41, which gives every adult an express right to vote in all elections
questions.explanation: Sections 7 and 24 require members of parliament to be directly chosen by the people, which the Court held protects against laws that disenfranchise people without a substantial reason. The High Court has read section 41 very narrowly.

questions.stem: Which provision protects the right of Queenslanders to vote and be elected at periodic state and local government elections?
options: Section 116 of the Australian Constitution
Section 5 of the Peaceful Assembly Act 1992 (Qld)
Section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth)
Section 23 of the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld)
questions.explanation: Section 23 protects the right to take part in public life, including voting and being elected at state and local elections. Because it is statutory, it is weaker than the constitutional protection that sections 7 and 24 give to federal elections.

questions.stem: A person is tried in the District Court of Queensland for an indictable offence against Commonwealth law. Under section 80 of the Constitution, as interpreted in Cheatle v The Queen (1993), the jury's verdict must be:
options: unanimous
by a majority of 11 to 1
by a majority of 10 to 2
by a simple majority of jurors
questions.explanation: The High Court held in Cheatle that trial by jury under section 80 requires a unanimous verdict. Queensland allows majority verdicts for most state offences, but not for Commonwealth offences tried on indictment.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates section 80 of the Constitution as a protection of the right to trial by jury?
options: It guarantees a jury for every criminal charge heard in any Australian court
It allows an accused to choose a judge alone for any Commonwealth offence
It protects jury trials for state offences as well as Commonwealth offences
It is entrenched, but parliament decides which offences are tried on indictment
questions.explanation: Section 80 applies only to trials on indictment for Commonwealth offences, and the High Court has accepted that parliament decides which offences are indictable, so many can be dealt with summarily. In Brown v The Queen (1986) the Court held an accused cannot waive a jury under section 80.

questions.stem: How many human rights does the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld) protect?
questions.explanation: The Act protects 23 human rights in sections 15 to 37, mostly civil and political rights drawn from the ICCPR, plus the rights to education and health services. The UDHR has 30 articles.

questions.stem: A man believes a Queensland government department breached his human rights. Before the Queensland Human Rights Commission will normally accept his complaint, he must:
options: lodge a complaint with the UN Human Rights Committee in Geneva
complain to the department and wait at least 45 business days
obtain a declaration of incompatibility from the Supreme Court of Queensland
show that the department has also breached the Anti-Discrimination Act
questions.explanation: Section 65 of the Human Rights Act requires the person first to complain to the public entity, and at least 45 business days must pass without an adequate response, unless exceptional circumstances apply. The Commission then tries to resolve the complaint, for example by conciliation.

questions.stem: The Queensland Human Rights Commission cannot resolve a human rights complaint against a public entity through conciliation. What happens next under the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld)?
options: The public entity is automatically fined, and the complainant receives the fine
The Commissioner reports on the complaint, but no tribunal decides it or awards damages
The complaint is referred to QCAT, which can award compensation to the complainant
The complaint is referred to the High Court, which decides whether the right was breached
questions.explanation: If a human rights complaint is not resolved, the Commissioner prepares a report (section 88), which may include recommendations. There is no referral to a tribunal for decision, and section 59 rules out damages for unlawfulness under section 58. Discrimination complaints, by contrast, can go to QCAT.

questions.stem: Section 59 of the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld) lets a person raise a breach of the Act in court only if they already have another legal ground to challenge a public entity's decision. This is often described as:
options: an 'override', which removes the Act from a particular law
a 'piggyback' cause of action, which limits access to court remedies
a 'stand-alone' cause of action, which lets anyone sue for damages
a 'class action', in which seven or more people sue together
questions.explanation: The Act does not create an independent right to sue; the human rights claim must be attached to another claim, such as judicial review. This is a common criticism of the Act as a means of enforcing rights.

questions.stem: In Johnston v Carroll (2024), the Supreme Court of Queensland declared COVID-19 vaccination directions issued by the Police Commissioner unlawful under the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld). Why?
options: The Act prohibits any public health measure that limits a person's freedom of movement
The directions were inconsistent with a Commonwealth law, so section 109 applied
The Commissioner had no power to make any directions to police officers
The Commissioner had not given proper consideration to human rights before making them
questions.explanation: Section 58(1)(b) makes it unlawful for a public entity, in making a decision, to fail to give proper consideration to a relevant human right. The court found the Commissioner had not done so. The Act allows rights to be reasonably limited, so it does not ban all public health measures.

questions.stem: Under section 48 of the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld), a court interpreting a Queensland statutory provision must:
options: interpret it compatibly with human rights, consistently with its purpose
declare it invalid if it is not compatible with every right protected by the Act
refer it to the Legislative Assembly whenever it might limit a human right
ignore its purpose and adopt whichever meaning gives the widest protection to rights
questions.explanation: Section 48 requires statutory provisions to be interpreted compatibly with human rights to the extent possible consistent with their purpose. It does not affect the validity of laws that cannot be read compatibly.

questions.stem: The Supreme Court of Queensland finds that a provision cannot be interpreted compatibly with human rights and makes a declaration of incompatibility. What is the effect?
options: The provision is invalid from the date of the declaration until parliament amends it
The person affected is entitled to damages from the State for the breach of their rights
The declaration is sent to the High Court, which decides whether the provision survives
The provision stays valid, but the Minister must table it and respond in parliament
questions.explanation: Under section 54 a declaration of incompatibility does not affect the provision's validity or create any right to damages. The responsible Minister must table it within 6 sitting days and table a written response within 6 months (section 56), so the final decision stays with parliament. This is called a dialogue model.

questions.stem: Under section 43 of the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld), parliament may make an override declaration in an Act. Which statement about an override declaration is correct?
options: It permanently removes a right from the Act for every Queensland law
It is for exceptional circumstances and expires after five years unless re-enacted
It can be made only by the Supreme Court after a declaration of incompatibility
It requires approval at a referendum of Queensland electors before it takes effect
questions.explanation: An override declaration lets an Act operate despite incompatibility with human rights. Parliament intends it only for exceptional circumstances, the member must explain them to the Assembly, and the declaration expires after five years unless re-enacted (section 45).

questions.stem: In 2023 the Queensland Parliament made override declarations so that children could be held in police watch houses, despite concerns this breached their human rights. Which statement best evaluates this?
options: It shows the Act is entrenched, because the override needed a two-thirds majority
It shows the courts can strike down overrides that breach children's rights
It shows the override was invalid, because watch houses are a Commonwealth matter
It shows the Act protects rights only as far as parliament chooses
questions.explanation: Because the Human Rights Act is an ordinary statute, parliament can override it by majority. Critics, including the Queensland Human Rights Commissioner, argued this weakened protection for children; supporters cited capacity pressures in youth detention. Courts cannot invalidate an override.

questions.stem: A Queensland woman's discrimination complaint about the provision of goods and services under the Anti-Discrimination Act 1991 (Qld) is not resolved by conciliation at the Queensland Human Rights Commission. Where can it be referred for a decision?
options: The Queensland Law Reform Commission
The Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal
The Court of Appeal of Queensland
The Australian Human Rights Commission
questions.explanation: Unresolved complaints under the Anti-Discrimination Act can be referred, at the complainant's request, to QCAT, or to the Queensland Industrial Relations Commission if the complaint is work-related. The tribunal can make binding orders, including compensation.

questions.stem: The Australian Human Rights Commission terminates a complaint under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) because conciliation has failed. What can the complainant do next?
options: Ask the Commission to make a binding order requiring the respondent to pay compensation
Appeal to the High Court, which hears all discrimination complaints at first instance
Ask QCAT to review the Commission's decision to terminate the complaint
Apply to the Federal Court or Federal Circuit and Family Court within 60 days
questions.explanation: The Commission resolves complaints by conciliation but cannot make binding determinations. After termination, the complainant can apply to the Federal Court or the Federal Circuit and Family Court within 60 days of the notice, or later with the court's permission.

questions.stem: Which method of seeking to resolve a human rights issue is a formal legal process rather than an informal or political one?
options: Starting an online petition about the issue
Lodging a complaint with a human rights commission
Joining a street march outside Parliament House
Writing to a local member of parliament
questions.explanation: Lodging a complaint starts a process set out in legislation, such as conciliation by a commission, which can lead to a tribunal or court. Protest, lobbying and petitions are legitimate ways to raise awareness and pressure law-makers but have no legal outcome themselves.

questions.stem: Which is a function of the Australian Human Rights Commission?
options: Investigating and conciliating complaints under federal discrimination laws
Making binding orders that award damages for unlawful discrimination
Prosecuting people charged with criminal offences involving discrimination
Striking down Commonwealth laws that breach international human rights treaties
questions.explanation: The Commission, established in 1986, investigates and conciliates complaints, holds public inquiries, educates the community, reports to parliament and may intervene in court cases with permission. Only courts and tribunals make binding orders.

questions.stem: The Australian Human Rights Commission's Respect@Work inquiry (2020) on sexual harassment led parliament to place a positive duty on employers to prevent it. This best shows the Commission:
options: using an inquiry and report to influence parliament to change the law
using its power to amend the Sex Discrimination Act without parliament
using its judicial power to hand down a binding precedent on harassment
using a referendum to give workers a constitutional right to safety
questions.explanation: The national inquiry, led by the Sex Discrimination Commissioner, consulted widely and recommended reforms, and parliament later amended the Sex Discrimination Act. The Commission advises and reports; only parliament can change legislation.

questions.stem: In Coco v The Queen (1994), the High Court held that a Queensland approval to use a listening device did not authorise police to enter private premises, because the Act did not clearly say so. This illustrates that courts protect rights by:
options: applying the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld) to cases decided before it was passed
referring the law to the Queensland Law Reform Commission for amendment
presuming parliament does not remove basic rights without clear words
striking down any Queensland law that allows police to use listening devices
questions.explanation: This is the principle of legality: courts read statutes as not interfering with fundamental rights, such as freedom from trespass, unless parliament makes its intention unmistakably clear. It protects rights through interpretation, but parliament can still remove them with clear words.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant limitation on courts as protectors of human rights in Australia?
options: They have no power to decide whether Commonwealth laws are constitutionally valid
They must follow the views of UN treaty bodies, even where these conflict with statutes
They can act only when a case is brought, and parliament can change the law in response
They cannot interpret laws, so they must apply every statute literally
questions.explanation: Courts are reactive: they need a party with standing and the resources to litigate, and parliament can generally override their interpretations by legislation. They can, however, invalidate laws that exceed constitutional limits and interpret laws to protect rights.

questions.stem: The Queensland Council for Civil Liberties (QCCL) mainly protects human rights by:
options: drafting bills on request from the Attorney-General as an official law reform body
prosecuting police officers who breach the rights of people they arrest
making submissions to parliamentary committees and public comment
hearing complaints and making binding orders against Queensland government agencies
questions.explanation: The QCCL is an independent, volunteer-based organisation that advocates for civil liberties, for example by commenting on bills about police powers, protest and youth justice. It has no power to decide complaints or prosecute, and it is not a government law reform body.

questions.stem: The Human Rights Law Centre is best known for which method of advancing human rights?
options: Strategic litigation, along with policy advocacy and engagement with UN bodies
Conciliating discrimination complaints under Commonwealth anti-discrimination law
Reviewing government decisions on their merits as a tribunal established by statute
Providing emergency food and shelter after natural disasters and armed conflicts
questions.explanation: The Human Rights Law Centre is an independent non-profit that runs test cases to set legal precedents, advocates for law reform and reports to UN bodies. Complaint conciliation is the role of human rights commissions, and disaster relief is the work of groups such as the Red Cross.

questions.stem: Australian Lawyers for Human Rights is best described as:
options: a UN body that monitors Australia's compliance with the ICCPR
a network of lawyers promoting human rights through advocacy and education
a government agency that provides free lawyers to everyone charged with a crime
a court that hears appeals in human rights cases from state tribunals
questions.explanation: Australian Lawyers for Human Rights is a non-government association of lawyers that makes submissions, educates the profession and public, and promotes the use of human rights law in Australia. Legal aid commissions, not ALHR, provide publicly funded lawyers.

questions.stem: Amnesty International mainly works to protect human rights by:
options: making binding rulings in disputes between states about human rights
researching abuses and campaigning to pressure governments to act
sending peacekeeping troops to countries where abuses are occurring
trying individuals accused of crimes against humanity in its courts
questions.explanation: Amnesty International, founded in 1961, investigates and documents abuses and mobilises its members through campaigns, letters and media to pressure governments. It received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977. It has no military or judicial powers.

questions.stem: In 2016 several Australian churches offered sanctuary to asylum seekers facing return to offshore detention and campaigned publicly for them to stay. This best shows church groups:
options: using legal powers to overturn decisions made under the Migration Act
acting as tribunals that review immigration decisions on their merits
drafting legislation that parliament is required to pass unchanged
using moral authority and public campaigns to advocate for human rights
questions.explanation: Church groups advocate through public statements, campaigns, direct support services and their moral standing in the community. Sanctuary has no legal force, so their influence is persuasive rather than legal.

questions.stem: The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, which includes the Australian Red Cross, mainly protects human rights by:
options: lobbying for one political party that supports human rights legislation
deciding complaints about discrimination by Queensland employers
coordinating humanitarian relief and promoting humanitarian principles and law
prosecuting soldiers who breach the Geneva Conventions in its own courts
questions.explanation: The IFRC coordinates national Red Cross and Red Crescent societies in disaster relief, health and community services, guided by principles of humanity, impartiality and neutrality. National societies also promote international humanitarian law. Neutrality means they do not support political parties.

questions.stem: A television investigation exposes mistreatment of people in a Queensland facility, and the government quickly announces an inquiry. Which statement best evaluates the media's role in protecting human rights?
options: It can expose abuses and prompt action, but coverage may be selective or sensational
It is the most effective protector, because its reports are binding on governments
It has no role, because only courts can decide whether human rights are breached
It can only report a court's decisions, not investigate matters for itself
questions.explanation: Investigative journalism can reveal hidden abuses and create pressure for inquiries and reform. However, media coverage depends on newsworthiness and ownership interests, may simplify complex issues and can fade quickly, so its influence is uneven.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares the Australian Law Reform Commission and the Australian Human Rights Commission?
options: The ALRC handles discrimination complaints; the AHRC drafts all Commonwealth bills
Both can make binding orders requiring the government to change its laws
The ALRC is a non-government group; the AHRC is a court of law
The ALRC recommends law reform on referral; the AHRC also handles complaints
questions.explanation: The ALRC conducts inquiries referred by the Attorney-General and recommends changes, including on how laws affect rights. The AHRC promotes and protects rights through complaints, inquiries and education. Neither makes binding orders, and both are independent statutory bodies.

questions.stem: A student analyses a proposed Queensland law banning protests within 50 metres of a mine site. Which step best shows evaluation using legal criteria?
options: Stating the date on which the bill was introduced into the Legislative Assembly
Weighing whether the limit on assembly is justified by its safety aim
Listing the names of the groups that have organised protests at the mine site
Describing how many people attended each protest in the past twelve months
questions.explanation: Evaluation weighs viewpoints and consequences against legal criteria such as justice, the rule of law and whether a limit on rights is reasonable and demonstrably justified, as section 13 of the Human Rights Act requires. Listing facts identifies the issue but does not evaluate it.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld) as a means of protecting rights in Queensland?
options: It has no effect, because public entities are not required to consider human rights
It protects rights only in Commonwealth courts and tribunals sitting in Queensland
It improves scrutiny and decision-making, but it can be overridden and offers no damages
It is the strongest possible protection, because courts can invalidate any incompatible law
questions.explanation: The Act requires statements of compatibility, rights-compatible interpretation and proper consideration of rights by public entities. But as an ordinary statute it can be overridden, courts can only declare incompatibility, and section 59 limits remedies, including no damages.
